name: Viprostol

card.summary: An experimental topical prostaglandin E2 analog (CL-115347) that was tested in men with pattern hair loss as a possible way to grow hair back.
card.note: Investigational compound; not an approved or marketed hair-loss treatment.

quick.overview:
Viprostol is a synthetic analog of prostaglandin E2 that can be absorbed through the skin. Prostaglandins are signalling lipids, and researchers in the late 1980s tested viprostol on the scalp as a possible treatment for male pattern baldness, with the appearance goal of denser hair.

The one published randomised trial in men with androgenetic alopecia reported that hair counts fell in all groups, including the viprostol group, over 24 weeks, and its authors concluded the compound was not an effective hair growth promoter. Most other research on viprostol concerns blood pressure and blood vessels.
quick.how: In the trial, a topical viprostol preparation was applied to the scalp twice daily for six months and compared with vehicle and placebo, with hair counted from macrophotographs. It was developed as a research compound and is not available as a hair-loss product.
quick.risks: Viprostol was studied as a skin-applied antihypertensive, where it produced vasodilation and a modest drop in diastolic pressure together with compensatory rises in renin, aldosterone and norepinephrine and sodium retention. It is not an approved medicine, and there is no standard consumer product.

lead: Viprostol (code name CL-115347) is a synthetic analog of prostaglandin E2, a vasodilating signalling molecule. It was designed to be given through the skin and was developed mainly as an antihypertensive [1][3][5].

For appearance, viprostol was examined as a topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia. In a randomised, double-blind study of 57 men, viprostol, vehicle or placebo was applied twice daily for 24 weeks; non-vellus hair counts declined in all three groups, and the authors concluded it was not effective as a hair growth promoter [2].
Beyond that trial, the published literature deals with its skin absorption and metabolism, its blood-vessel effects in animals and humans, and in-vitro effects on fat cells [1][3][4][5][6][7].

chain: Prostaglandin E2 analog applied to the scalp
angle.text: The idea was to use a skin-penetrating prostaglandin to regrow scalp hair in men with pattern baldness. The one controlled trial reported no increase in hair counts.

infobox: Antihypertensive; also tested for male pattern baldness

paras: Viprostol is a methyl ester of a modified prostaglandin E2 and was described as transdermally active, with research on how it is absorbed through the skin and metabolised in skin [1].

In anaesthetised dogs, it increased blood flow in several vascular beds, and in spontaneously hypertensive rats its antihypertensive effect persisted when other pathways were blocked, which the authors read as direct vasodilation similar to natural PGE2 [5]. Experiments in genetically hypertensive rats also examined its renal vascular effects [4]. In isolated rat fat cells it inhibited catecholamine-stimulated lipolysis in vitro [7].

Hair loss: a randomised, double-blind trial assigned 57 men with androgenetic alopecia to viprostol, vehicle or placebo twice daily for 24 weeks. Hair growth was judged by patients and investigators and by counts from macrophotographs. Counts declined in all three groups, and the authors concluded viprostol was not an effective hair growth promoter [2].

Blood pressure: in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 26 people with essential hypertension, transdermal CL-115347 lowered diastolic pressure by about 7.8 mm Hg versus 2.3 mm Hg in controls, with compensatory increases in renin, aldosterone and norepinephrine and sodium retention [3]. In patients with congestive heart failure, a viprostol-induced fall in blood pressure was accompanied by a fivefold rise in plasma renin activity [6].

The hypertension study reported compensatory hormonal and renal responses, including sodium retention, to chronic administration, and described the blood pressure effect as modest [3]. The hair-loss trial abstract does not report adverse event details [2].

timeline.event: Mechanism studies describe viprostol as a vasodilating prostaglandin antihypertensive; a clinical trial tests transdermal CL-115347 in hypertension [3][5].
Review of viprostol's transdermal absorption and skin metabolism published [1].
Randomised trial reports viprostol did not improve hair counts in androgenetic alopecia [2].
